title: The Ten Commandments
share: What did God say at Sinai, and what did Yeshua say about it? Nine steps through the ten words, Exodus 20 beside Deuteronomy 5.
opening_question: What did God say at Sinai, and what did Yeshua say about it? Read the ten words in Exodus 20 beside Deuteronomy 5, what Yeshua said about the law, and what Paul and James say about love and the law. Christians number the commandments differently and apply them differently, the Sabbath most of all. Each reading is shown with its own verses, and BibleChat gives no verdict.

steps.question: Before any commandment, what does God say about who He is and what He has done? What does the Bible call these words, and where were they written?
steps.apply: Do I obey God to earn His love, or because He has already brought me out?

facts.text: The first words are not a command but who He is: "I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt".
"the ten commandments" is in Hebrew the ten words: dabar is "a word", "a matter". The Bible never numbers them one by one.
They were "tables of stone, written with the finger of God".

steps.question: What do the first words say about other gods and graven images? To whom does God show mercy "unto thousands"?
steps.apply: What do I bow down to, or serve, in place of God?

facts.text: "Thou shalt have no other gods before me." Then: "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image"; pesel is "an idol".
"visiting the iniquity" reaches "unto the third and fourth generation"; "shewing mercy" reaches "unto thousands of them that love me".

Christians count the ten in different ways, all from these same verses. In Jewish tradition the first word is "I am the LORD thy God" and other gods and images are the second. Catholics and Lutherans join other gods and images as the first and count the coveting of the wife and of the goods as two. The Orthodox and most Protestants count other gods first, images second, and coveting as one. BibleChat gives no verdict.

steps.question: What does it mean to take the name of the LORD "in vain"? What does He say about the one who does it?
steps.apply: How do I use His name when I speak, promise or pray?

facts.text: "take" is nasa: "to lift", to carry. "vain" is shav: "uselessness", "false", "lie". It covers more than cursing: carrying His name falsely or emptily.
"the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain."

steps.question: Read the Sabbath commandment in Exodus beside Deuteronomy. What reason does each give for the day?
steps.apply: When do I stop and rest, and who else can rest because I do?

facts.text: Exodus begins "Remember the sabbath day" and gives creation as the reason: "For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth".

Deuteronomy begins "Keep the sabbath day" and gives Egypt as the reason: "remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt", and adds "that thy manservant and thy maidservant may rest as well as thou."

Christians apply this commandment in different ways: some keep the seventh day, some keep the first day, the Lord's day, and some hold that the rest is fulfilled in Christ. The three-part Study Path The Sabbath: God's day of rest (in Foundations) walks through every passage. BibleChat gives no verdict here.

steps.question: What does God promise to the one who honours father and mother? How does Paul repeat this commandment?
steps.apply: How can I honour my parents, living or not, this week?

facts.text: "Honour" is kabad: "to be heavy", to make "weighty". To honour is to give weight to.
Paul repeats it and calls it "the first commandment with promise".

steps.question: What do the next four words protect? How did Yeshua take "Thou shalt not kill" and "Thou shalt not commit adultery" into the heart?
steps.apply: Where has anger or a look already crossed a line in my heart?

facts.text: Four short words: life, marriage, property and truth. "kill" is ratsach: "especially to murder". The BSB and the Ethiopian Canon read "You shall not murder."
"false witness": sheqer is "an untruth", "a sham".

Yeshua: "whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment", and "whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart."

steps.question: The last word is about desire, not deeds. What may we not covet? How does the order differ in Deuteronomy, and what did this commandment show Paul?
steps.apply: What do I want so much that it has started to own me?

facts.text: "covet" is chamad: "to delight in", "desire". The same word describes Eden's trees as "pleasant to the sight".
Exodus names "thy neighbour's house" first; Deuteronomy names "thy neighbour's wife" first and uses a second verb, "desire".
Paul: "I had not known lust, except the law had said, Thou shalt not covet."

steps.question: What did Yeshua say He came to do with the law? When asked for the great commandment, which two did He name?
steps.apply: Which of the two great commandments do I find harder today?

facts.text: "I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil." "fulfil" is pleroo: "to make replete", to "fill (up)", "finish", "complete".
"one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled."

Both great commandments come from the Law of Moses: "thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart" and "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself". "On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets."

steps.question: How do Paul and James sum up the commandments? What does Jeremiah say God will do with His law in the new covenant?
steps.apply: Which commandment do I most need God to write on my heart?

facts.text: Paul lists five of the ten and sums them up: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself". "love is the fulfilling of the law."
James: "whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all." He calls it "the law of liberty".
God's promise: "I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts". First on stone, then on the heart.

Christians differ on how the ten apply to believers today. Some hold that all ten are binding as written, the seventh-day Sabbath included. Some hold that the moral law stands and the Sabbath is kept on the Lord's day or fulfilled in Christ. Many add that keeping the law does not save, but shows love for the One who saves. Each reading points to these verses; BibleChat gives no verdict.
